Tool Learning Needs Nothing More Than
A Free 8B Language Model

Chenming Tang    Hsiu-Yuan Huang    Weijie Liu    Junqiang Zheng Affiliation: LLM Department, Tencenttangchenming@stu.pku.edu.cn  jagerliu@tencent.com  wuyf@pku.edu.cn    Saiyong Yang Affiliation: LLM Department, Tencenttangchenming@stu.pku.edu.cn  jagerliu@tencent.com  wuyf@pku.edu.cn    Yunfang Wu Affiliation: National Key Laboratory for Multimedia Information Processing, Peking University Affiliation: School of Computer Science, Peking University    *Work done during an internship at Tencent  Corresponding authors
Abstract

Reinforcement learning (RL) has become a prevalent paradigm for training tool calling agents, which typically requires online interactive environments. Existing approaches either rely on training data with ground truth annotations or require advanced commercial language models (LMs) to synthesize environments that keep fixed once created. In this work, we propose TRUSTEE, a data-free method training tool calling agents with dynamic environments fully simulated by free open-source LMs that can be as small as 8B, including task generation, user simulation, tool simulation and trajectory evaluation, paired with an adaptive curriculum learning mechanism that controls various aspects of the task difficulty dynamically during training. Our empirical results show that TRUSTEE brings consistent improvements across various domains and outperforms all the baselines which require extra external resources for training. These confirm that, with a sufficiently sophisticated design, even simulated environments with a local 8B LM as the backbone could set a strong baseline for tool learning, without expensive annotated data, realistic human interactions, executable tools or costly verifiable environments from human experts or commercial LMs. We hope our proposed paradigm could inspire future research on environment scaling with limited resources.

1 Introduction

Tool calling, also known as function calling, enables language models (LMs) to interact with the external environment. Thereafter, LMs have become active agents that can have access to external information Zhuang et al. (2023), make use of realistic services Patil et al. (2024); Schick et al. (2023), and even make changes to the world Yao et al. (2023).

With the prevalence of agentic reinforcement learning (agentic RL) Jin et al. (2025), more and more work has been focusing on teaching LMs to call tools (i.e., tool learning) via RL. Earlier work directly adopt data for supervised fine-tuning (SFT), which requires ground truth annotations, for single-turn reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards (RLVR) Qian et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2025b); Zeng et al. (2025). However, due to the cost and limited availability of real-world tools and users, when it comes to truly online multi-turn RL, there is a significant challenge in scaling the environment11 1 In this paper, environment refers to all the external components for the agent, including users, tools and other entities like an optional verifier., for that such kind of RL requires a large number of online interactions including calling many tools and dynamically interacting with the user, which has also challenged evaluation Ruan et al. (2024); Guo et al. (2024) and SFT data construction Fang et al. (2025); Chen et al. (2025); Liu et al. (2025).

One approach of environment scaling is to apply LMs but most of these work only partially simulates the environment (simulates either the tools Sullivan et al. (2025); Castellani et al. (2025); Li et al. (2026) or the users Qian et al. (2025b)) and relies on existing data or environments (i.e., supports some specific tasks only). For instance, Simia-RL Li et al. (2025) simulates the responses of tools with LMs during interactions, but requires established data containing training tasks as the input (e.g., τ\tau-bench Yao et al. (2025)) and does not support the multi-turn interaction between the agent and the user. Another approach is to make use of synthesized code and databases Song et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026), but such approach requires a complex generation pipeline for high-quality synthesis using expensive commercial LMs and the generated environments and tasks are fixed once created, which may be too easy for strong agents but overly difficult for weak ones.

To this end, we introduce TRUSTEE, Tool leaRning Using SimulaTEd Environments, a data-free method training tool calling agents with a local open-source LM as the only required resource. TRUSTEE uses an LM to generate the task, simulate the user, simulate tool responses, and evaluate the trajectories, which provides complete environments for tool learning while independent of any existing training data or tasks, human annotations or interactions, realistic executable tools, or verifiable environments engineered by experts or commercial LMs. Moreover, we design an Adaptive Curriculum Learning (ACL) mechanism that takes the advantage of the dynamically controllable nature of the simulated environments and tasks, which controls the difficulty of the tasks in various aspects based on the reward of the last step adaptively and ensures a smooth learning process for the tool calling agent.

Our empirical evaluation validates the effectiveness of TRUSTEE. The Qwen3-8B LM, when trained solely with environments simulated by itself, outperforms all the baselines which either require annotated data or need advanced commercial LMs to synthesize or instantiate the environments. This proves that, with sufficiently sophisticated designs, simulated environments may serve as a powerful approach to tool learning that can even beat realistic data or synthesized verifiable environments.

Our contributions include:

  • •

    We introduce TRUSTEE, a paradigm of simulating every environment component with an LM for RL-based tool learning, paired with adaptive curriculum learning that dynamically keeps the tasks and environments at an appropriate difficulty for the agent.

  • •

    We run computational experiments and demonstrate the effectiveness of TRUSTEE, confirming even a fully simulated environment with an 8B open-source LM can lead to a competitive tool calling agent.

  • •

    We validate that tool learning does not necessarily require established data, realistic human interactions, executable tools, and verifiable environments from human experts or commercial LMs, moving a step towards cost-friendly tool learning.

Our code will be publicly available when this work is completely finished.

2 Method

2.1 Problem Formulation

We formalize the tool calling agent task as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP) Zhang et al. (2026), defined by the tuple:

⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒫,ℛ,γ,𝒪⟩,\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{P},\mathcal{R},\gamma,\mathcal{O}\rangle, (1)

where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the state space, 𝒜=𝒜text∪𝒜tool\mathcal{A}=\mathcal{A}_{\text{text}}\cup\mathcal{A}_{\text{tool}} is the action space (textual response or tool calling), 𝒫\mathcal{P} is the state transition probability, ℛ\mathcal{R} is the reward space, γ\gamma is the discount factor, and ℛ\mathcal{R} is the observation space. At the tt-th step, the agent receives an observation ot=O⁡(st)o_{t}=O(s_{t}) based on the state st∈𝒮s_{t}\in\mathcal{S}, takes an action at∈𝒜a_{t}\in\mathcal{A} based on its policy πθ\pi_{\theta} and the observation oto_{t}, receives a reward rt=R⁡(st,at)r_{t}=R(s_{t},a_{t}), and the environment transitions according to P⁡(st+1∣st,at)P(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}).

The initial objective of POMDP is to maximize the discounted cumulative reward:

𝒥POMDP​(θ)=𝔼τ∼πθ[∑t=0T−1γt​rt].\mathcal{J}_{\text{POMDP}}(\theta)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\gamma^{t}r_{t}\right]. (2)

In this work, we focus on the final reward instead due to practical considerations:

𝒥ours​(θ)=𝔼τ∼πθ[rτ].\mathcal{J}_{\text{ours}}(\theta)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\tau\sim\pi_{\theta}}\left[r_{\tau}\right]. (3)

2.2 Fully Simulated Environment

Our fully simulated environment is demonstrated in Figure 1. There are three stages for each training step. The first stage is to generate tasks for this batch (§ 2.2.1). The second stage is to perform simulated interaction to collect trajectories (§ 2.2.2). The last stage is to reward the trajectories and optimize the policy (§ 2.2.3).

2.2.1 Task Generation

At the nn-th training step, for each task 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i}, we first sample a subset ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} of a large repository of tools ℱ\mathcal{F}. The size of the subset is determined by the current task difficulty 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} (see § 2.3):

ℱi=Sample​(ℱ,𝒟n).\mathcal{F}_{i}=\text{Sample}(\mathcal{F},\mathcal{D}_{n}). (4)

In practice, the tool repository can be from various sources like existing datasets, crawled tools from the Internet, manually designed tool sets, etc. Note that the tools only consist of basic textual information including names and parameters and do not have to be actually executable functions.

Then, we generate the task based on the sampled tools ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} and current difficulty 𝒟n\mathcal{D}_{n} using a task generator Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}} instantiated by an LM:

𝒯i=Φtask​(ℱi,𝒟n)=(pi,gi,qi,ci),\mathcal{T}_{i}=\Phi_{\text{task}}(\mathcal{F}_{i},\mathcal{D}_{n})=(p_{i},g_{i},q_{i},c_{i}), (5)

where pip_{i} is the user persona, gig_{i} is the user intent (i.e., the ultimate goal of the task), qiq_{i} is the first user query to trigger an interaction, and cic_{i} is the expected tools to be called to finish the task.

2.2.2 Simulated Interaction

We perform simulated interaction based on the generated tasks. The interaction environment includes a tool executer Φtool\Phi_{\text{tool}} and a user Φuser\Phi_{\text{user}}, both simulated by an LM.

For each task 𝒯i\mathcal{T}_{i} at training step nn, we sample MM interaction trajectories. In each trajectory, after receiving the first observation o0=τ=(qi)o_{0}=\tau=(q_{i}), the agent LM θ\theta begins to interact with both the tool executer and user by generating actions made up of tokens x1≤j≤|at|x_{1\leq j\leq|a_{t}|} based on the current observation oto_{t} (which is equivalent to the current trajectory τ\tau in the LM agent scenario) and available tools ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i}:

at=πθn​(ot,ℱi)={xj}j=1|at|,a_{t}=\pi_{\theta}^{n}(o_{t},\mathcal{F}_{i})=\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{|a_{t}|}, (6)

which will be appended to the trajectory of this task:

τ=τ⊕at.\tau=\tau\oplus a_{t}. (7)

If ata_{t} is a tool calling, the simulated tool Φtool\Phi_{\text{tool}} will be called to generated a simulated tool result based on the current interaction history, the available tools for the agent and the user intent:

ft=Φtool​(τ,ℱi,gi),f_{t}=\Phi_{\text{tool}}(\tau,\mathcal{F}_{i},g_{i}), (8)

which will be appended to the trajectory as well:

τ=τ⊕ft.\tau=\tau\oplus f_{t}. (9)

Otherwise, if ata_{t} is a textual response to the user, the simulated user Φuser\Phi_{\text{user}} will be called to generate a user message based on the current interaction history, the available tools for the agent, the user intent and the user persona:

ut=Φuser​(τ,ℱi,gi,pi),u_{t}=\Phi_{\text{user}}(\tau,\mathcal{F}_{i},g_{i},p_{i}), (10)

which will be appended to the trajectory as well:

τ=τ⊕ut.\tau=\tau\oplus u_{t}. (11)

Then, the observation of the next step ot+1o_{t+1} will be updated as the current trajectory τ\tau.

The user simulator may choose to end the task by generating an empty response if it believes there is no need to perform more interactions. Otherwise, the interaction will continue until the sequence length or the interaction turn reaches a pre-defined limit.

Optionally, the simulators may return an immediate reward rtr_{t} for step-level rewarding. But we does not use these rewards because we observed they did not work well in our earlier experiments.

2.2.3 Rewarding and Optimization

For each sampled trajectory τm\tau_{m}, when the interaction is finished, a verifier Φreward\Phi_{\text{reward}} instantiated by an LM is called to evaluate the whole trajectory and generates a final reward based on the available tools for the agent, the user intent, the user persona, the expected tools to be called and the current task difficulty (which indicates the evaluation criteria):

rm=Φreward​(τm,ℱi,gi,pi,ci,𝒟n).r_{m}=\Phi_{\text{reward}}(\tau_{m},\mathcal{F}_{i},g_{i},p_{i},c_{i},\mathcal{D}_{n}). (12)

When all the criteria are met, the trajectory receives a positive reward (i.e., 1 in this work). When most criteria are met, the verifier only gives a neutral reward (i.e., 0 in this work). If there are severe errors or the criteria are scarcely met, there will be a negative reward (i.e., -1 in this work).

In this work, we choose GRPO Shao et al. (2024) (with token-level loss Yu et al. (2025)) as our optimization algorithm due to its relative stability and simplicity:

𝒥GRPO(θ)=𝔼𝒯i∼𝒯[1Z∑m=1M∑t=0Tm−1∑j=1|at|(CLIP(rm,t,j(θ),A^m,t,j,ε)−βDKL(πθ∥πref))],\mathcal{J}_{\text{GRPO}}(\theta)=\mathop{\mathbb{E}}_{\mathcal{T}_{i}\sim\mathcal{T}}\left[\frac{1}{Z}\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{m}-1}\sum_{j=1}^{|a_{t}|}\left(\operatorname{CLIP}(r_{m,t,j}(\theta),\hat{A}_{m,t,j},\varepsilon)-\beta\,\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}})\right)\right], (13)

where ZZ is the normalization factor:

Z=∑m=1M∑t=0Tm−1|at|,Z=\sum_{m=1}^{M}\sum_{t=0}^{T_{m}-1}|a_{t}|, (14)

rm,t,j​(θ)r_{m,t,j}(\theta) is the importance sampling ratio:

rm,t,j​(θ)=πθ​(xm,t,j∣τm,<t,x<j)πθold​(xm,t,j∣τm,<t,x<j),r_{m,t,j}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}\bigl(x_{m,t,j}\mid\tau_{m,<t},\,x_{<j}\bigr)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\bigl(x_{m,t,j}\mid\tau_{m,<t},\,x_{<j}\bigr)}, (15)

A^m,t,j\hat{A}_{m,t,j} is the group-relative advantage based on the final reward only:

A^m,t,j=rm−Mean⁡({rm}m=1M)Std⁡({rm}m=1M),\hat{A}_{m,t,j}=\frac{r_{m}\;-\;\mathrm{Mean}\bigl(\{r_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}\bigr)}{\mathrm{Std}\bigl(\{r_{m}\}_{m=1}^{M}\bigr)}, (16)

and DKL(πθ∥πref)\mathrm{D}_{\mathrm{KL}}(\pi_{\theta}\|\pi_{\text{ref}}) is the KL penalty term.

2.3 Adaptive Curriculum Learning (ACL)

An advantage of the fully simulated environment is that every component of it is dynamic and adjustable in an online manner, which naturally enables adaptive curriculum learning which keeps a moderate difficulty for the current policy and ensures good learnability.

2.3.1 Task Difficulty

We control the difficulty of tasks in the following aspects.

Number of Available Tools

The number of tools in ℱi\mathcal{F}_{i} sampled from ℱ\mathcal{F} directly determines the overall difficulty. The larger number of available tools for the agent, the harder for the agent to make use of tools properly and precisely. On the contrary, if there is only one tool available, the agent will have no trouble choosing tools.

Number of Expected Tool Callings

The more expected times of tool calling which is passed to the task generator Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}}, the more complex the generated task will be.

Turns of Interactions

If a task requires more interaction turns, it is naturally more difficult and complex. Therefore, we use the number of expected turns, which will be passed to the task generator Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}} to design the task based on the expectation, to control the difficulty. Meanwhile, the maximum number of interaction turns also evolves dynamically with the expected turns for more efficient training.

System Prompt

We expect the agent learns to perform high-quality tool calling under a general system prompt and make the specificity of the system prompt for the agent gradually decrease during training. To this end, we design system prompts at different degrees of specificity. The most specific system prompt describes the overall multi-turn tool calling task in detail with hands-on instructions of how to perform reasoning and how to call tools in a correct format (a few paragraphs). Then, a more concise system prompt presents the core notes (a few sentences) regarding the agentic task only. After that, a highly consolidated system prompt states the task in a sentence (e.g., “You are a helpful multi-turn dialogue assistant capable of leveraging tool calls to solve user tasks.”). Finally, the hardest system prompt is the most general one (i.e., “You are a helpful assistant.”), with no special descriptions regarding any specific task, which may make the agent unsure of what to do if it is less familiar with tool calling.

Persona of User

Typically, a less expert user makes the task harder due to a lower level of knowledge Barres et al. (2025). Therefore, we design three kinds of user personas: expert, beginner, and novice. Then, we use this as an input to the task generator Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}} which generates a more specific description of the user persona pip_{i}, ensuring the diversity.

Ambiguity of Query

If a user query is ambiguous, it may confuse the agent and require it to ask for further clarification from the user, which makes the task harder and more realistic. Therefore, we employ three ambiguity degrees: clear, somewhat ambiguous, and highly ambiguous. Then, we use this as an input to the task generator Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}} which generates a user query based on the requirements.

Criteria of Rewarding

A stricter evaluation criteria naturally makes it harder for the agent to obtain a high reward. We increase the difficulty by gradually taking more criteria into consideration when calling the verifier simulator Φreward\Phi_{\text{reward}}. The verifier gives a positive reward only when all the criteria are met. Concretely, we design five levels of criteria: meeting user intent, using expected tools correctly, no hallucination, no redundant trials, and efficiency. These draw a step-by-step path to a perfect tool-calling agent.

2.3.2 Difficulty Evolution

The difficulty is updated after each training step based on the overall reward of the finished batch. If the averaged reward r¯n\bar{r}_{n} of training step nn is higher than a threshold ηhigh\eta_{\text{high}}, the difficulty level for the next step 𝒟n+1\mathcal{D}_{n+1} will increase by a step size δ\delta. If the reward is lower than a threshold ηlow\eta_{\text{low}}, 𝒟n+1\mathcal{D}_{n+1} will decrease by δ\delta:

𝒟n+1={𝒟n+δif ​r¯n>ηhigh𝒟n−δif ​r¯n<ηlow𝒟notherwise.\mathcal{D}_{n+1}=\begin{cases}\mathcal{D}_{n}+\delta&\text{if }\bar{r}_{n}>\eta_{\text{high}}\\ \mathcal{D}_{n}-\delta&\text{if }\bar{r}_{n}<\eta_{\text{low}}\\ \mathcal{D}_{n}&\text{otherwise}\end{cases}. (17)

Then, all of the aspects described in § 2.3.1 will be derived based on 𝒟n+1\mathcal{D}_{n+1}. In this work, we design a large value range (e.g., from 1 to 100) for 𝒟n+1\mathcal{D}_{n+1} and convert it to the scales of different aspects. For example, since the range of user persona is 0-2 (0 for expert, 1 for beginner, and 2 for novice), the derived user persona level will be ⌊𝒟n+1×0.02⌋\lfloor\mathcal{D}_{n+1}\times 0.02\rfloor. In this way, the user persona will be expert for difficulty from 1 to 49, beginner for difficulty from 50 to 99, and novice for difficulty 100.

Since the difficulty works for every task in a batch, the batch may converge to a specific pattern of tasks, which hurts the diversity during training. For example, a detailed system prompt is always paired with an expert user. To this end, we apply a soft design of curriculum, which does not always follow the current difficulty strictly. To be specific, for each task, there is a probability of ϵ\epsilon to sample the tool number, the expected tool callings, the interaction turns, the user persona, and the query ambiguity randomly within the current difficulty. In this way, the task patterns can be more diverse.

3 Experimental Setup

3.1 Data

Evaluation Benchmarks

We evaluate baselines and our method on the Berkeley Function Calling Leaderboard (BFCL) V4 Patil et al. (2025) and τ2\tau^{2}-bench Barres et al. (2025). The former tests various aspects of tool calling for agents comprehensively and the latter evaluates interactive tool calling in three realistic scenarios.

Tool Repository

We instantiate our tool repository ℱ\mathcal{F} using the tools collected by ToolBench Qin et al. (2024), which are representational state transfer (REST) APIs gathered from RapidAPI22 2 https://rapidapi.com/hub with detailed descriptions, spanning 49 diverse categories like social media, e-commerce, and weather. Besides this tool repository, we do not need any specific data for training.

3.2 Language Model

We focus on the Qwen3 Yang et al. (2025) herd of language models, which is widely used for reinforcement learning in the community. To be specific, we experiment with Qwen3-8B as the agent LM. We also use Qwen3-8B as the backbone LM for simulation (including Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}}, Φtool\Phi_{\text{tool}}, Φuser\Phi_{\text{user}}, and Φreward\Phi_{\text{reward}}).

3.3 Baselines and Methods

Our evaluated baselines and methods include: (1) Original Model: the agent LM before training. (2) ToolRL Qian et al. (2025a): a single-turn reinforcement learning from verifiable reward (RLVR) method using existing data Zhang et al. (2025a); Liu et al. (2025); Lin et al. (2025) with ground truth annotations. (3) Tool-N1 Zhang et al. (2025b): another single-turn RLVR method using existing data Zhang et al. (2025a); Liu et al. (2025) with ground truth annotations. (4) Simia-RL Li et al. (2025): an online multi-turn training method that simulates the tool responses with commercial LMs and trains on τ\tau-bench Yao et al. (2025). (5) EnvScaler Song et al. (2026): a method that generates environments via programmatic synthesis using commercial LMs. (6) AWM Wang et al. (2026): another method that employs programmatic environment synthesis using commercial LMs. (7) TRUSTEE (Ours): our method training the agent in the environment simulated by an open-source LM.

3.4 Implementation Details

We experiment on a single node with 8×\times NVIDIA H20 GPUs. 4 GPUs are used for agent training and the other 4 are used for deploying the simulation LM. Our training script is developed on the basis of verl Sheng et al. (2025). The simulation backbone LM is deployed using vLLM Kwon et al. (2023).

To ensure the sampled tools from ℱ\mathcal{F} are not overly discursive, we prioritize tools from the same category (also randomly sampled) when sampling. We begin to sample from a new category only when all the tools are selected in the previous one.

The prompt templates used in our experiments are shown in Appendix A. The detailed descriptions of the task difficulty for adaptive curriculum learning are presented in Appendix B. The details of evaluation can be found in Appendix C. The hyper-parameters in our experiments are listed in Appendix D. The details of baseline methods are presented in Appendix E.

4 Results

4.1 Results of Single-turn Tool Calling

The results of single-turn tool calling (the Non-Live and Live subset of BFCL) are presented in Table 1. TRUSTEE exhibits the best performance across all the categories except “Simple” and secures the highest averaged metrics.

Since Qwen3-8B has already been good at tool calling with high initial scores, some baselines fail to further improve its tool calling capability. Simia, which is specially tuned for the τ\tau-bench, suffers from overfitting and degrades drastically on the general BFCL benchmark. Tool-N1, AWM and EnvScaler show degradation on certain subsets. ToolRL, although improves the average scores for both subsets, causes a sharp decline in the “Live Parallel Multiple” category. On the contrary, TRUSTEE ensures solid improvements in all the categories, even without any labeled data, verifiable environments, or advanced LMs.

4.2 Results of Multi-turn Tool Calling

The results of multi-turn tool calling (the Multi-Turn subset of BFCL and τ2\tau^{2}-bench) are presented in Table 2. TRUSTEE exhibits the best performance across all the categories except “Base” of BFCL’s “Multi-Turn” and “Airline” of τ2\tau^{2}-bench.

On “BFCL Multi-Turn”, TRUSTEE brings consistent improvements across all the categories. Simia suffers from overfitting and causes the LM to forget almost everything in this scenario while AWM does not necessarily improve the LM. The gain of ToolRL is also marginal. Tool-N1 and EnvScaler bring solid improvements but they require a lot more extra resources than TRUSTEE.

On τ2\tau^{2}-bench, all the baselines degrade on certain subsets, especially “Telecom”, and none improves the overall averaged score. This reveals their limited generalization. Our proposed TRUSTEE is the only method that improves the LM’s performance on all the subsets with the highest average score.

All the results validate the effectiveness of TRUSTEE. As a method requiring no extra resources like annotated data or commercial LMs, it exhibits the most outstanding performance across various evaluation aspects. These confirm that with a sufficiently sophisticated design of the simulated environment, tool learning requires nothing more than an open-source LM to serve as the environment backbone. For Qwen3-8B, this even means TRUSTEE needs nothing more than the LM itself.

5 Related Work

5.1 Tool Learning

Tool calling, also known as function calling, allows LMs to obtain information from the external environment Zhuang et al. (2023); Tang et al. (2023), make use of helpful utilities Schick et al. (2023); Patil et al. (2024), and interact with the real world Yao et al. (2023), which converts generative assistants to intelligent agents.

Tool learning aims to enhance the tool calling capability of LMs via training. Earlier research focuses on supervised fine-tuning, which requires high-quality offline data. ToolAlpaca Tang et al. (2023) generates user queries and tool responses using LMs to synthesize single-turn data. BUTTON Chen et al. (2025) and ToolACE Liu et al. (2025) simulates both the user and tools to collect multi-turn trajectories for SFT. AgentScaler Fang et al. (2025) instantiates tools as executable code and local databases and simulates the user with a user agent to collect multi-turn SFT data.

Search-R1 Jin et al. (2025) first introduces agentic reinforcement learning, which LMs learn to call tools (e.g., search engine APIs) via multi-turn reinforcement learning, which is superior in generalization. A lot of work performs reinforcement learning with verifiable feedback (RLVR) with existing SFT data Qian et al. (2025a); Zhang et al. (2025b); Zeng et al. (2025). To enable truly multi-turn online learning, recent work constructs environments with LM-simulated tools Li et al. (2025) or synthesized code and databases Cai et al. (2025); Song et al. (2026); Wang et al. (2026). Our work focuses on scaling the RL environment for tool learning with purely open-source LMs.

5.2 Environment Scaling for LM Agents

Real-world APIs are usually expensive and unstable Guo et al. (2024), limiting the scalability of tool environments. Therefore, it is necessary to scale the environment for tool calling agents via simulation or synthesis. ZeroSearch Sun et al. (2025) replaces the search engine API in Search-R1 with an LM. Simia-RL Li et al. (2025) simulates tool responses in the online interactions with LMs. GTM Ren et al. (2025) trains a specific LM to simulate tool responses. AutoForge Cai et al. (2025), EnvScaler Song et al. (2026) and AWM Wang et al. (2026) automatically generate user intents and build environments in the form of executable code and local databases for online reinforcement learning. Our work instantiates the whole environment as an LM and takes the advantage of adaptive curriculum learning.

6 Limitations

Our work has certain limitations. First, the scalability of the simulated environment is constrained due to the bounded capability of the simulation LM, which may not generate sufficiently complex tasks or sufficiently accurate rewards when the task involves a large number of tools and a lot of turns of interactions. Second, there are a lot of hyper-parameters required in our method, especially those in the adaptive curriculum learning, which makes it difficult to find an optimal setup. Third, due to the instability of LMs, sometimes the simulation LM itself fails to generate a valid response and causes a lot of aborted trajectories, which may hurt the stability of the training.

7 Discussion

We have presented TRUSTEE, a data-free method that simulates all the environment components for online tool learning. Empirical results show that TRUSTEE brings consistent improvements across various domains of tool calling and outperforms all the compared baselines, which rely on either annotated data or environments synthesized by advanced commercial LMs. Our work proves that, with a proper design, fully simulated environments can effectively train tool calling agents even with a local open-source 8B LM as the backbone while requiring no annotated data or tasks.

This work is still in progress. Future work includes: (1) exploring other approaches of credit assignment to take advantage of the turn-level rewards in our simulated environment and improve the training with denser supervision; (2) perform ablation study on TRUSTEE to analyze the contribution of each component; (3) employ different LMs as the simulator and analyze the effect of the simulator choice; (4) incorporating advanced entropy-controlling techniques to mitigate the entropy collapse during training; (5) providing a theoretical foundation for this study.

Appendix A Prompt Templates

The prompt templates for Φtask\Phi_{\text{task}}, Φtool\Phi_{\text{tool}}, Φuser\Phi_{\text{user}}, and Φreward\Phi_{\text{reward}} are presented in Figure 2 - 5.

Appendix B Details of Task Difficulty

The detailed descriptions of the different difficulty aspect at all levels are presented in Table 3. Note that the rewarding criteria are applied in an incremental manner. The criteria at level ll should include all those from level 00 to level ll.

Appendix C Details of Evaluation

For BFCL V4, we follow the default evaluation setup and do not further extend the maximum context size of the LM for long-context scenarios.

For τ2\tau^{2}-bench, we adopt GPT-4.1 as the user simulator following [25]. The maximum number of interaction turns is 64 in our experiments due to limited budget.

Appendix D Hyper-parameters

D.1 Training

The hyper-parameters for training are listed in Table 4. The batch size is only 16 because a larger batch size requires a higher level of concurrency which may cause the local vLLM server for the simulation LM overloaded.

D.2 Curriculum

The step size of difficulty evolution δ\delta is 3. The probability of soft curriculum ϵ\epsilon is 0.5. The reward thresholds for difficulty update ηlow\eta_{\text{low}} and ηhigh\eta_{\text{high}} are 0.0 and 0.5, respectively.

The range of the number of tools is 1-10. The range of the expected tool callings is 1-3. The ranges of the expected turns, maximum user turns, maximum tool turns, maximum agent turns are 1-2, 1-3, 1-3, 1-6, respectively.

Appendix E Details of Baselines

ToolRL

We reproduce ToolRL based on their released scripts33 3 https://github.com/qiancheng0/ToolRL (we do not directly run theirs due to model incompatibility) with aligned maximum sequence length. We ran the training for 500 steps with a batch size of 32 to align the overall training time. However, the training process collapsed soon after 400 steps. Therefore, we evaluate the checkpoint of 400 training steps.

Tool-N1

We reproduce ToolRL based on their released scripts44 4 https://github.com/NVlabs/Tool-N1 (we do not directly run theirs due to model incompatibility) with aligned maximum sequence length. We run the training for 500 steps with a batch size of 32 to align the overall training time.

Simia-RL

We evaluate their released checkpoint55 5 https://huggingface.co/Simia-Agent/Simia-Tau-SFT-RL-Qwen3-8B trained using Qwen3-8B directly. We do not re-run their training script because Simia-RL is currently limited to a few scopes like τ\tau-bench and requires expensive commercial LM for training.

EnvScaler

We train the LM with the provided scripts66 6 https://github.com/RUC-NLPIR/EnvScaler and the default hyper-parameters. We focus on the pure RL setting and thus train the model from scratch without SFT, which is in line with TRUSTEE and many other baselines.

AWM

We evaluate their released checkpoint77 7 https://huggingface.co/Snowflake/Arctic-AWM-8B trained using Qwen3-8B directly because no training script is released.
